parts: Consumer protection means safeguarding consumers against unfair trade practices and exploitation by producers, traders and service providers, and providing remedies when they are cheated. It is needed because of consumer ignorance, unorganised consumers, widespread exploitation, the huge variety of goods, misleading advertisements, and because services cannot be checked before buying. National Consumer Day is observed on 24 December (the day the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 was passed).

(1) Adulteration — mixing something inferior into the product (argemone in mustard oil, papaya seeds in black pepper, kerosene in petrol). (2) Sale of spurious products — fake goods sold as genuine, often medicines. (3) False weights and measures — goods weighed or measured short, sweets weighed with the box. (4) Sale of duplicates — goods carrying marks of superior quality or well-known brands that they are not. (5) Hoarding and black-marketing — holding back stocks to create artificial scarcity, then selling secretly above the fixed price. (6) Sale of sub-standard goods that do not meet prescribed safety standards. (7) Tie-in sales — forcing the purchase of another product with the one wanted. (8) Misleading advertisements — falsely claiming superior quality (an air purifier claiming to remove 100% germs). (9) Gifts and lotteries that are not genuine; poor after-sales service; overcharging above MRP.

Consumers — self-help is the best help: know and assert their rights, form associations. Businessmen — supply quality goods at fair prices, avoid malpractices, settle complaints, follow fair trade; trade associations and chambers of commerce act against members who cheat. Government — pass and enforce laws, set up consumer courts, include consumer representatives in policy bodies, run awareness campaigns (Jago Grahak Jago). Businesses cannot say nothing can be done, and the government is not indifferent.

Agricultural Products (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937 — grading and certification of agricultural products with the AGMARK seal. Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 — control over production and distribution of manufactured goods. Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 — severe punishment for adulteration of food. Essential Commodities Act, 1955 — control of production, supply and price of essential goods; action against hoarders and black-marketers. Standards of Weights and Measures Act, 1956 (and 1976) — standard metric weights and measures. MRTP Act, 1969 — action against restrictive and unfair trade practices. Prevention of Black-marketing and Maintenance of Essential Supplies Act, 1980. Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 — BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) sets quality standards and certifies products with the ISI mark (electrical appliances); hallmark for jewellery. Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (COPRA) — the most comprehensive law: six consumer rights, three-tier consumer courts and cheap, quick redressal for goods and services; replaced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

Under the 1986 Act (as in the NIOS book): District Forum — claims up to ₹20 lakh; State Commission — above ₹20 lakh up to ₹1 crore, and appeals against District Forums; National Commission (New Delhi) — above ₹1 crore, and appeals against State Commissions; appeals against the National Commission go to the Supreme Court. Under the 2019 Act as revised in 2021: District Commission up to ₹50 lakh; State Commission ₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore; National Commission above ₹2 crore. The Supreme Court is not a consumer court.

A consumer or a consumer association files a written complaint (with the cash memo and other documents) within two years of the cause of action, by post or in person, with a nominal fee. Cases are to be decided within three months, or five months if the product needs laboratory testing. Reliefs (directions to the opposite party): remove the defect or deficiency; replace the goods; refund the price; pay compensation for loss or injury; stop the unfair practice; withdraw hazardous goods; pay corrective advertising.

Voluntary, non-profit bodies such as the Consumer Guidance Society of India (Mumbai) and CERC (Ahmedabad). They educate consumers through seminars and workshops; give legal aid and file cases on their behalf; represent consumers on official bodies; test competing products comparatively and publish results; publish journals; and suggest new laws and policies to government.
